intro: Long ago, surfers in California had a problem. Some days the ocean had no waves. So people put roller-skate wheels under a wooden board. They rolled on the sidewalk instead.
In this unit, you will learn how the skateboard began. You will meet the parts of a board. You will learn the job of each part, from the deck to the tiny bearings.
By the end, you can tell the story of the first boards. You can point to each part and say what it does. You can check a board with a grown-up before a ride.
bigQuestion: How did people make a board that rolls, and what does each part do?

Stores begin to sell ready-made skateboards
Larry Stevenson starts making Makaha skateboards
First national skateboard championships in Anaheim, California
Champion Patti McGee is on the cover of Life magazine
Frank Nasworthy sells soft plastic wheels called Cadillac Wheels
Carlsbad Skatepark in California and Skateboard City in Florida open
Skateboarding is added to the Olympic Games
Skateboarding is in the Olympics for the first time, in Tokyo, Japan

write.prompt: Tell how the skateboard began. Then pick two parts of a skateboard. Say what each part is and what job it does.

Say what the first boards were made of.
Use part names like deck, trucks, wheels or grip tape.

title: A Board With Wheels

chapters.title: Surfing on the Sidewalk
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a day with no waves lead to the skateboard?

story.title: A Day With No Waves
story.kicker: The ocean is flat and still. What can a surfer do now?
paragraphs: Mia stands on a beach in California. She holds her dad's hand. They came to watch the surfers. But the ocean is flat today. There are no big waves. The water just laps at the sand.
The surfers sit on the beach. Their long boards lie in the sand. One surfer sighs. "No waves today," he says. Mia looks at the quiet water. She wonders, "What does a surfer do now?"
Then Mia hears a rumble. A boy rolls by on the path. He stands on a small wooden board. It has little wheels under it. He leans, and the board turns. He looks like he is riding a wave!
Mia's dad smiles. "Long ago, surfers did that too," he says. "When the waves were flat, they surfed the sidewalk." Mia watches the boy roll away. She wants to learn how that board began.
story.think: If you could not do your favorite thing today, what would you make or try instead?

lessons.title: Surfers in California
lessons.mainIdea: Surfers in California wanted to surf even when the ocean had no waves.
reading: California is a state by the ocean. In the 1950s, many people there loved to *surf*. To surf, you stand on a long board. A wave pushes you toward the beach.
Surfers need waves. Some days the ocean is flat. A flat ocean has no big waves. On flat days, the surfers had nothing to ride. They had to wait on the sand.
Waiting was hard for them. They wanted to feel that ride every day. So some of them asked a question. Could they ride a board on land?

words.d: to ride a wave on a long board in the ocean
smooth and even, with no bumps or big waves

look.title: Two Days at the Beach
look.text: Picture the beach on Monday. Tall waves roll in. Surfers ride them to the sand. Now picture the beach on Tuesday. The water is smooth like glass. The surfers sit and wait.
look.prompt: On which day could the surfers ride? What could they do on the other day?

check.q: What does a surfer need to ride in the ocean?
check.why: A wave pushes the surfer and board toward the beach. No waves means no ride.

check.q: What is a flat ocean like?
check.why: A flat ocean is smooth. It has no big waves to ride.

check.q: Where did these surfers live?
check.why: The reading says many people in California, a state by the ocean, loved to surf in the 1950s.

lessons.title: Wheels Under a Board
lessons.mainIdea: People made the first skateboards by putting roller-skate wheels under a wooden board.
reading: Long ago, kids had *roller skates*. Roller skates have wheels on the bottom. Some people took the wheels off old skates. They fixed the wheels under a flat piece of wood.
Now the wood could roll! A person could stand on it. That board with wheels was an early *skateboard*. Many people made their own at home.
Who made the very first one? Nobody knows for sure. People tell many stories about it. But no one person is known as the inventor.

words.d: shoes or frames with wheels on the bottom
a board with wheels that you stand on and ride

look.title: Building a Board Long Ago
look.text: Look at the old roller skate on the floor. It has four small metal wheels. Now look at the plank of wood beside it. Picture the wheels moved from the skate to the bottom of the wood. The plank can roll now.
look.prompt: Where did the wheels on the first boards come from?

check.q: What did people put under a wooden board to make it roll?
check.why: People took wheels from roller skates and fixed them under a flat board.

check.q: Who made the very first skateboard?
choices: A famous surfer named in every book
check.why: There are many stories, but no one person is known as the inventor.

check.q: Where were many early skateboards made?
check.why: Many people made their own boards at home with wood and skate wheels.

lessons.title: Sidewalk Surfing
lessons.mainIdea: People called the new ride sidewalk surfing because it felt like surfing on land.
reading: Riders stood on the board like a surfboard. They leaned one way, and the board turned. They leaned the other way, and it turned back. It felt like riding a wave.
So people gave it a name. They called it *sidewalk surfing*. A *sidewalk* is the path next to a street where people walk.
This was in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Many early riders rode with bare feet, like surfers. Today riders wear flat shoes to grip the board.

words.d: an early name for skateboarding, because it felt like surfing on land
the hard path next to a street where people walk

look.title: Lean and Turn
look.text: Picture a rider rolling slowly on a flat path. She bends her knees. She leans her body a little to one side. The board curves that way. She leans back to the middle. The board goes straight again.
look.prompt: Stand up and pretend to ride. Which way do you lean to make a turn?

check.q: Why was it called sidewalk surfing?
choices: It was done in the ocean
It felt like surfing, but on land
check.why: Riders leaned and turned like surfers, but on paths instead of waves.

check.q: How did a rider turn the board?
check.why: Leaning one way made the board turn that way.

check.q: What do riders wear on their feet today?
check.why: Today riders wear flat shoes so their feet grip the board.

lessons.title: Bumpy Old Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Early skateboard wheels were hard and bumpy, so small stones could stop them.
reading: The first wheels were made of metal or clay. They were very hard. They did not grip the ground well. They made a loud, rattling sound.
Hard wheels feel every bump. A tiny *pebble* could stop a wheel fast. Then the rider might tip off the board. Riding was shaky and slow.
Later, people made wheels from softer stuff. Softer wheels roll over small bumps. The ride got smoother and quieter.

words.d: a small, smooth stone
a round part that turns so a thing can roll

look.title: The Little Stone
look.text: Picture a board with metal wheels rolling down a path. Rattle, rattle, rattle. Ahead sits one small stone. The front wheel hits it. The wheel stops. The board stops too.
look.prompt: What happened when the hard wheel hit the stone? Why?

check.q: What were the first skateboard wheels made of?
check.why: The first wheels were metal or clay. They were very hard.

check.q: What could a tiny pebble do to a hard wheel?
check.why: Hard wheels feel every bump. A pebble could stop the wheel and tip the rider.

check.q: Why do softer wheels ride better?
check.why: Softer wheels roll over small bumps instead of stopping.

lessons.title: Boards in Stores
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1959, stores began to sell skateboards that were already made.
reading: At first, people built their own boards. Then companies started making skateboards. Around 1959, you could buy one in a *store*.
A store board was ready to ride. You did not need old skates or a saw. More kids could get a board this way.
Soon, lots of kids were riding. By the mid-1960s, there were skateboard teams and contests. A *contest* is a game where people try to do their best.

words.d: a place where you buy things
an event where people try to do their best and someone wins

check.why: Stores began selling ready-made boards around 1959.

choices: They were ready to ride, with no building

check.q: What is a contest?
choices: An event where people try their best and someone wins
check.why: A contest is an event where people try to do their best.

lessons.title: Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Today people skateboard in countries all over the world.
reading: Skateboarding began in California. Now people skate all over the *world*. Kids skate in Brazil. Kids skate in Japan. Kids skate in England and in Illinois.
In 2021, skateboarding was in the *Olympics* for the first time. The Olympics are big games with people from many countries. The games were in Tokyo, Japan.
Some winners were only 13 years old. Momiji Nishiya of Japan won a gold medal. Rayssa Leal of Brazil won silver in the same event. Sky Brown of Great Britain won bronze in park skating.

words.d: all the lands and countries on Earth
big sports games with people from many countries

check.why: Skateboarding began in California. It spread all over the world.

check.q: When was skateboarding first in the Olympics?
check.why: Skateboarding was first in the Olympics in 2021, in Tokyo, Japan.

check.q: Who won a gold medal at age 13?

lessons.title: Then and Now
lessons.mainIdea: Skateboards changed a lot, but riders still lean, roll and balance.
reading: An old board was a plank of wood. It had hard metal or clay wheels. Riders often had bare feet and no helmets.
A board today has a curved deck and soft wheels. Riders wear flat shoes. Skaters today wear a *helmet* that fits and is buckled.
Some things did not change. You still stand on a board. You still lean to turn. You still need *balance*, which means staying steady so you do not tip.

words.d: a hard hat that protects your head
staying steady so you do not tip over

look.title: Two Boards Side by Side
look.text: Look at two boards on a table. The old one is a flat plank. Its wheels are small and metal. The new one curves up at both ends. Its wheels are wide and smooth. Both boards have four wheels.
look.prompt: Name one way the boards are different and one way they are the same.

check.q: What does balance mean?
choices: Staying steady so you do not tip
check.why: Balance means staying steady so you do not tip over.

check.q: What do skaters wear on their heads today?
choices: A helmet that fits and is buckled
check.why: A helmet that fits and is buckled protects your head.

check.q: What is the same on old and new boards?
choices: You lean to turn on both
check.why: Riders still stand on the board and lean to turn, then and now.

review.q: What were early skateboards made from?

review.why: Stores began selling ready-made boards around 1959.
Skateboarding started in California and spread to countries all over the world.

chapters.title: The Parts of a Skateboard
chapters.bigQuestion: What does each part of a skateboard do?

story.title: The Board on the Table
story.kicker: A skateboard lies upside down. Can the class name every part?
paragraphs: Mr. Diaz walks into class. He carries a skateboard under his arm. He sets it on a table upside down. The four wheels point up at the ceiling. The class leans in close.
"Let's find every part," says Mr. Diaz. Jada points to the flat wood. "That is where you stand!" Omar spins one wheel with his finger. It whirs around and around.
Lin finds the metal parts that hold the wheels. Sam turns the board over. The top feels rough under his hand. "Like sandpaper!" he says. Mr. Diaz nods and smiles.
"Every part has a job," says Mr. Diaz. "If one part is missing, the board will not ride well." The class wants to learn each job. They start at the top.
story.think: Which part of the board would you want to touch first? Why?

lessons.title: The Deck
lessons.mainIdea: The deck is the board you stand on.
reading: The big flat part is the *deck*. You stand on the deck. Your feet go on top of it. The deck holds you up while you roll.
Most decks are made of wood from maple trees. Thin sheets of wood are glued together. Most decks have seven thin sheets. The sheets make the deck strong but light.
A deck is not perfectly flat. It dips down a little in the middle. The dip helps your feet stay on the board.

words.d: the board of a skateboard that you stand on
a kind of tree with hard, strong wood

look.title: Stand on the Deck
look.text: Look at a skateboard lying flat on soft grass. It cannot roll on the grass. A boy steps on the middle of the deck. He sets one foot down, then the other. He bends his knees. He stands still and steady.
look.prompt: Pretend the floor is a deck. Where would your feet go?

check.q: What part of the skateboard do you stand on?
check.why: The deck is the flat board you stand on.

check.q: What are most decks made of?
choices: Thin sheets of maple wood glued together
check.why: Most decks are made of thin sheets of maple wood glued together, often seven.

check.q: Why does the deck dip a little in the middle?
choices: To help your feet stay on
check.why: The small dip in the middle helps your feet stay on the board.

lessons.title: Nose and Tail
lessons.mainIdea: The nose is the front end of the deck, and the tail is the back end.
reading: A deck has two ends. The front end is the *nose*. The back end is the *tail*. Both ends curve up a little.
The tail is very useful. When you step down on the tail, the nose lifts up. Skaters use the tail to turn and to start tricks.
The nose and tail can look almost the same. Often the nose is a little longer and curves up a little more. Some skaters mark the nose so they can tell.

words.d: the front end of a skateboard deck
the back end of a skateboard deck

look.title: Press the Tail
look.text: Picture a board resting on a carpet. It is not rolling. A girl puts her foot on the tail. She presses down gently. The tail goes down and touches the carpet. The nose rises up into the air.
look.prompt: What happens to the nose when you press the tail? Show it with your hand.

check.q: What is the front end of the deck called?
check.why: The front end is the nose. The back end is the tail.

check.q: What happens when you press down on the tail?
check.why: Stepping on the tail pushes it down, so the nose lifts up.

check.q: Which end is often a little longer?
check.why: The nose is often a little longer than the tail.

lessons.title: Rough Grip Tape
lessons.mainIdea: Grip tape is rough like sandpaper so your shoes do not slip.
reading: Rub your hand on top of a deck. It feels rough and scratchy. That is *grip tape*. It is a sticky sheet that covers the top of the deck.
Grip tape is rough like *sandpaper*. Your shoes rub on it and hold tight. So your feet do not slide off when the board moves.
Grip tape works best when it is dry. Water makes it slippery. Skate on dry days, in dry places.

words.d: a rough, sticky sheet on top of the deck that keeps shoes from slipping
rough paper used to rub wood smooth

look.title: Slippery or Grippy?
look.text: Picture two boards. One has no grip tape. Its top is smooth, shiny wood. Your shoe slides across it. The other board has grip tape. Your shoe presses down and stays put.
look.prompt: Which board would you want to stand on? Why?

check.q: What does grip tape feel like?
check.why: Grip tape is rough and scratchy, like sandpaper.

check.q: What is grip tape for?
check.why: Your shoes hold tight on the rough grip tape, so your feet do not slide.

check.q: Where is the grip tape?
check.why: Grip tape covers the top of the deck, where your feet go.

lessons.title: The Trucks
lessons.mainIdea: Trucks are the metal parts that hold the wheels and help the board turn.
reading: Turn a skateboard upside down. You will see two metal parts. These are the *trucks*. One truck is near the nose. One truck is near the tail.
Each truck holds two wheels. Small *bolts* hold each truck onto the deck. Riders put their feet over the bolts to stand steady.
Trucks also help you turn. When you lean, the trucks tilt. Then the wheels point a new way, and the board turns.

words.d: the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and help the board turn
small metal pins with nuts that hold the trucks onto the deck

look.title: Lean to Turn
look.text: Look at a board upside down on a table. A teacher presses on one side of the deck. Watch the truck. It tilts a little. The wheels turn to point a new way. When she lets go, they point straight again.
look.prompt: Lean your body to one side. Which way would the board turn?

check.q: How many trucks are on a skateboard?
check.why: There is one truck near the nose and one near the tail. That makes two.

check.q: What holds a truck onto the deck?
check.why: Small bolts hold each truck onto the deck.

check.q: What do trucks do when you lean?
choices: They tilt so the board turns
check.why: When you lean, the trucks tilt. The wheels point a new way and the board turns.

lessons.title: Four Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: A skateboard rolls on four wheels, two on each truck.
reading: A skateboard has four *wheels*. Two wheels are on the front truck. Two wheels are on the back truck. Four wheels keep the board steady.
Wheels today are made of a soft, strong plastic. They roll smooth and quiet. They hold on to the ground well. Old metal wheels could not do that.
Some wheels are softer. Soft wheels roll well on rough sidewalks. Some wheels are harder. Hard wheels slide more easily at a skatepark.

words.d: the four round parts that roll on the ground

look.title: How Many Wheels?
look.prompt: Which one has the most wheels? How many more than a bike?

check.q: How many wheels does a skateboard have?
check.why: A skateboard has four wheels, two on each truck.

check.q: What are wheels today made of?
check.why: Wheels today are a soft, strong plastic. They roll smooth and quiet.

check.q: Which wheels roll well on a rough sidewalk?
check.why: Soft wheels roll well over rough sidewalks.

lessons.title: Bearings Help Wheels Spin
lessons.mainIdea: Bearings are small rings inside the wheels that help them spin.
reading: Look inside the middle of a wheel. You will see a small metal ring. That is a *bearing*. Each wheel has two bearings, one on each side.
Inside a bearing are tiny steel balls. The balls roll around and around. They help the wheel spin fast and easy. Without bearings, the wheel would rub and stick.
Bearings do not like water or sand. Water can make them rust. Sand can make them grind. Keep your board dry and clean.

words.d: a small metal ring with tiny balls inside that helps a wheel spin

look.title: Spin the Wheel
look.text: Picture a board upside down. A girl flicks one wheel with her finger. It spins and spins. It keeps going for a long time. It makes a soft whirring sound. The bearings inside help it turn.
look.prompt: Why does the wheel keep spinning after she lets go?

check.q: Where are the bearings?
choices: Inside the middle of each wheel
check.why: Bearings sit inside the middle of each wheel, one on each side.

check.q: What is inside a bearing?
check.why: Tiny steel balls roll inside the bearing and help the wheel spin.

check.q: What can water do to bearings?
check.why: Water can make bearings rust, so keep your board dry.

lessons.title: Counting the Parts
lessons.mainIdea: Each part has a job, and a board needs all of them to ride safely.
reading: Let's count the parts. One deck holds you up. Two trucks hold the wheels and help you turn. Four wheels roll. Eight bearings help the wheels spin.
Each part has a *job*. If a wheel is loose, the board may wobble. If a bolt falls out, a truck can come loose. A board needs every part.
Before you ride, check your board with a grown-up. Spin each wheel. Look at each bolt. Then put on your helmet and buckle it.

words.d: the work a thing or a person does
to look closely to make sure something is OK

look.title: Parts on One Skateboard
look.prompt: Which part does a board have the most of? Why are there two of them for each wheel?

check.q: How many bearings are on one skateboard?
check.why: Each of the four wheels has two bearings. That makes eight.

check.q: What might happen if a wheel is loose?
check.why: A loose wheel can make the board wobble. Every part needs to be tight.

check.q: What should you do before you ride?
choices: Check your board with a grown-up
check.why: Check the wheels and bolts with a grown-up, then put on a buckled helmet.

review.q: Which part is the board you stand on?
review.why: You stand on the deck, the big flat board.

review.q: What is the back end of the deck called?
review.why: The tail is the back end. The nose is the front end.
Rough grip tape holds your shoes so your feet do not slide off.

review.q: Which parts hold the wheels and help you turn?
review.why: The trucks hold the wheels. They tilt when you lean so the board turns.

review.q: What helps the wheels spin fast and easy?
review.why: Bearings have tiny steel balls inside that help the wheels spin.

review.q: How many wheels are on one skateboard?
review.why: A skateboard has four wheels, two on each truck.
